title: Jeremiah 32:26–35
context: Jeremiah 32:26–35 is the LORD’s answer to Jeremiah’s prayer. He takes up Jeremiah’s own words and asks, "Is there anything too hard for me?" (compare Genesis 18:14, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?"). First he confirms the judgment: he will give the city to Nebuchadnezzar, and the Chaldeans will burn it with the houses where incense was offered to Baal. Israel and Judah have provoked him from their youth, every class has turned its back to him though he taught them persistently, they defiled his house with abominations, and they built high places in the valley of the son of Hinnom to make their children pass through fire to Molech, something he never commanded. Similar charges appear in 7:30–31 and 19:5. Both traditions read the unit as stating plainly why the judgment is just before the promise of restoration that follows.

verses.text: Then the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s word comes to Jeremiah in answer. Arminians see God responding to his servant’s honest prayer, which shows that he welcomes questions brought to him in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s answer as revealing his purposes. Both traditions read what follows as the LORD’s explanation of both the judgment and the restoration, which together answer Jeremiah’s question.

verses.text: “Behold, I am the LORD, the God of all flesh. Is there anything too hard for me?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he is the God of all flesh and asks whether anything is too hard for him. Arminian readers see God taking up Jeremiah’s words from verse 17 and affirming them, which gives the prophet confidence in the promise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign power over all creation. Both traditions compare Genesis 18:14, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" and hold this as shared ground about God’s ability to fulfill his word.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says: Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the Chaldeans, and into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will take it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will give the city to the Chaldeans and to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will take it. Arminians see God confirming that judgment is still coming, even though restoration will follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s control over the nations in judgment. Both traditions note that how God uses hostile powers is discussed at Judges 9:23, and they do not reopen that question here.

verses.text: The Chaldeans, who fight against this city, will come and set this city on fire, and burn it with the houses on whose roofs they have offered incense to Baal, and poured out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me to anger.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the Chaldeans will burn the city with the houses where incense was offered to Baal and drink offerings to other gods. Arminian readers see the judgment matching the sin, since the places of idolatry will be destroyed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s holiness in judging idolatry. Both traditions note that the burning of Jerusalem is narrated in 2 Kings 25:9 and Jeremiah 39:8 and 52:13.

verses.text: “For the children of Israel and the children of Judah have done only that which was evil in my sight from their youth; for the children of Israel have only provoked me to anger with the work of their hands, says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Israel and Judah have done only evil in his sight from their youth and provoked him with the work of their hands. Arminians see a long history of unfaithfulness, which shows God’s great patience before judgment finally came.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as describing the depth of human sin. Both traditions read the phrase from their youth as covering the nation’s whole history, and they note that the work of their hands likely refers to idols.

verses.text: For this city has been to me a provocation of my anger and of my wrath from the day that they built it even to this day, so that I should remove it from before my face,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the city has provoked his anger from the day it was built until now, so he should remove it. Arminian readers see strong language expressing God’s grief and anger over a city that should have been holy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s righteous anger against persistent sin. Both traditions read the words from the day that they built it as rhetorical emphasis on long-standing rebellion, not a denial of earlier faithful periods.

verses.text: because of all the evil of the children of Israel and of the children of Judah, which they have done to provoke me to anger—they, their kings, their princes, their priests, their prophets, the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the evil was done by kings, princes, priests, prophets, the men of Judah, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Arminians see guilt shared by all levels of society, from leaders to ordinary people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the list as showing that no group was innocent. Both traditions hold that leaders bear special responsibility, while the whole people share the guilt.

verses.text: They have turned their backs to me, and not their faces. Although I taught them, rising up early and teaching them, yet they have not listened to receive instruction.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they turned their backs and not their faces to him, though he taught them persistently, rising up early. Arminian readers see God’s patient teaching and the people’s real refusal, which makes their judgment just.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that the refusal was the people’s own and see God’s persistent appeals as gracious. Both traditions note that the phrase rising up early is a repeated image in Jeremiah for God’s earnest pleading (compare 7:13 and 25:3).

verses.text: But they set their abominations in the house which is called by my name, to defile it.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they set their abominations in the house called by his name to defile it. Arminians see the worst form of idolatry, where the people brought false worship into the very place devoted to the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the defilement of the temple as a sign of deep apostasy. Both traditions compare the same charge in 7:30 and the reforms of Josiah in 2 Kings 23, which did not change the people’s hearts.

verses.text: They built the high places of Baal, which are in the valley of the son of Hinnom, to cause their sons and their daughters to pass through fire to Molech, which I didn’t command them. It didn’t even come into my mind, that they should do this abomination, to cause Judah to sin.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they built high places of Baal in the valley of the son of Hinnom to make their children pass through fire to Molech, which he never commanded or thought of. Arminian readers see God strongly disowning child sacrifice, which shows that it was entirely contrary to his will.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the horror of this sin. Both traditions read the words it didn’t even come into my mind as an emphatic statement that God never commanded it, not as a limit on his knowledge, and they compare 7:31 and 19:5.
